lesson.title: Speaking the Same Language: How Protocols Make Networks Work
lesson.summary: A protocol is the precise, agreed-upon set of rules that lets independent devices on a network exchange information correctly, covering what messages look like, what they mean, and when they are sent.
lesson.body:
A computer network only becomes useful once the machines connected to it can actually understand each other, and that is the entire job of a protocol. A protocol is a precise, agreed-upon set of rules that governs how two or more devices exchange information: what messages look like, what each part of a message means, and in what order things must happen. Without a shared protocol, two computers plugged into the same cable or joined to the same Wi-Fi network are no more able to communicate than two people speaking mutually unintelligible languages seated at the same table.

Every protocol answers three separate questions, and a specification that only covers one of them is not actually usable. Syntax defines the structure of a message: how many bits are in a field, where the sender's address goes, where the real data begins. Semantics defines what each field and each message actually means: a certain field holding the value 6 might signal "this is TCP," while the value 17 signals "this is UDP." Timing defines the rules for sequencing and pacing: which side speaks first, how long to wait for a reply, and what to do if no reply ever arrives. Ambiguity in any one of these three areas is exactly where two otherwise compatible devices fail to talk to each other.

Consider what happens, concretely, when your laptop opens a connection to a web server, since it shows all three pieces working together. Your laptop sends a message with the SYN flag set, proposing a starting sequence number. If the server accepts, it replies with both the SYN and ACK flags set, acknowledging your number and proposing its own. Your laptop then sends a final ACK, confirming the server's number. Only after this three-step exchange, defined exactly by the TCP protocol, do either side treat the connection as open. Every detail is specified in advance: what the SYN flag means, what order the messages must arrive in, and what a device should do if it never receives a reply, which is to retransmit and eventually give up.

A single exchange across a computer network is rarely governed by just one protocol. Loading a web page involves HTTP, which governs how your browser asks for a resource and how the server answers, TCP, which governs how that request is broken up and delivered reliably, and a link-layer protocol like Ethernet, which governs how the resulting bits actually move across the wire in front of you. Each protocol solves one layer of the problem and hands its result to the next, and a network only functions as a coherent whole because these separate protocols were designed from the start to fit together.

This is also why a protocol cannot simply live in one engineer's head or one company's private source code. If a printer built by one manufacturer and a laptop built by an entirely different one are going to interoperate, the rules have to be written down precisely enough that both sides can implement them independently and still end up compatible. That written-down, formally agreed version of a protocol is what turns it into a standard, which is the subject of the next chapter.
